Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the left half of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16,$ shown above?
feedback.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{4y}{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4y}{x} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
